text:
Taki the Brewer was still sleeping, although the sun's rays had long since pierced the dirt-fogged windows of his stifling little room; the rays gradually illuminated his feet, crawled toward his paunch, glistened on his lower lip, dried and cracked by internal fire, rushed into his open mouth, and penetrated to the throat, from which waves of an ear-disturbing snoring broke forth. Just at that time, the postman knocked thrice on the door. But would Taki's ear understand such gentle signals? Had it been a weekday—so be it, but it happened to be a holiday. On the eve of a holiday, as you know, a person lets themselves go a bit more: a clink with this one, a clink with that one, and before you know it, they've gotten themselves quite pickled. And the same happened to Bai Taki: out of a desire to recommend his beer, he had gotten himself quite soaked. My point is, so to speak, so you won't wonder why the postman repeated the knocking on the door, and when no one answered, he delivered such soulless blows upon the innocent door that even if a whole cauldron of beer had visited Bai Taki's stomach, he would still have woken up. And wake up he did. He opened his eyes, squinted against the sun, and with a voice worthy of the throat from which it emerged, he asked:
— Who’s there?
— Mail — the postman replied, entered the room, stepped over to the bed, handed over a letter, and hurried to escape the stifling atmosphere of the unventilated bedroom.
Bai Taki coughed a bit, as is proper, rubbed his eyes, and unfolded the letter. An invitation!
"Honored Sir, you are requested to attend tomorrow, Sunday, at 5 o'clock in the afternoon, at the 'Suhindol Wines' warehouse, where the matter of founding a temperance society will be discussed."
Respectfully: For the initiators, Tanas Dochoolu, innkeeper

My God! How timely this invitation arrived. For Bai Taki’s parched throat and cracked lips were at that moment such agitators in favor of abstinence that he enthusiastically embraced the noble idea, and it only remained for the fifth hour after noon to arrive for him to declare himself the most ardent defender of abstinence. During the day, Bai Taki drank water. (To tell the truth—he did drink two small glasses of wine, but that’s just how the saying goes.) Whether five o'clock had struck or not, Bai Taki crossed the threshold of the vast "Suhindol Wines" warehouse.
— Is Uncle Tanas here? — he asked the boy who was standing behind the counter.
— Please, come in, they are here, in the little room — the boy answered respectfully and stepped forward to open the small door for him.

The host, Tanas Dochoolu, kindly welcomed his fellow and invited him to take a seat. Several citizens sat solidly and silently along the walls, inspired and drawn here by the noble idea of the future society. Bai Taki greeted everyone, and silence was restored once more, broken only by modest coughing. It was clearly visible that those gathered were waiting for a certain person, without whom they did not dare to open the meeting. Not much time passed before the outer doors opened. Dochoolu rushed to see if the desired guest was coming, but immediately returned with a dissatisfied look. Danko the Rogue burst into the room quite unexpectedly. "Just our luck!" whispered Bai Tanas to Bai Taki. It was evident that this was not the expected person. Danko opened his mouth to say something—and what would Danko's talk be: to curse someone; but no one showed a willingness to listen to him, and he fell silent. A few more minutes passed and (thank God!) the boy rushed headlong into the room and cried out as if frightened: "He's coming! He's coming!"
Everyone stood up. The outer doors opened and on the threshold appeared in all his majesty, in the original, our common friend Bay Ganyo Balkanski.

— Oh! Long live! — the long-awaited guest shouted enthusiastically, without specifying what "long live" referred to, but even without explanation, everyone understood that this referred to the future association.

— Long live! — the assembled group responded and began taking turns shaking Bay Ganyo's hand. Danko the Scoundrel, always less delicate, allowed himself (imagine that!) to pat Bay Ganyo on the neck, but Mr. Balkanski shot him such a look with his eyes that Danko tucked his tail and huddled in a corner. "Don't hold it against him, Bay Ganyo," the host whispered, "you know him. Danko is just Danko — a drunkard."

The meeting opened. Oh, gentlemen, if only you had the good fortune to find yourselves in that assembly! When those lips of Bay Ganyo gaped open, was it a man speaking or a nightingale singing... Wouldn't he convince you, Bay Ganyo? Why, not just about a society, but he could convince you to believe that Musala is your father and Vitosha is your mother... Forget it. Everyone was convinced that now was exactly the time to found a temperance society; only Danko Harsizina—to one's wonder and amazement—was a regular Doubting Thomas. Man, they spoke this way and that—no, he just sat in the corner, smirking under his mustache and dropping the occasional skeptical word. "It is time already to... such-and-such," orated Dochoolu, "to found... this-and-that... you understand, a society..." And Danko lets out a "never mind." "Drunkenness, honorable gentlemen," Bay Taki strung along, "reflects poorly on our work, on our health, on our offspring..." "Nonsense!" whispered Danko, smirking under his mustache. But the sun rises even without a rooster! We aren't going to abandon the sublime idea just because of one Danko. They left Danko to twirl his mustache and set about constituting the society. They decided to name the society "Temperance" and to ask the schoolmaster to write them a charter. The schoolmaster, willy-nilly, had to write the charter because, if you must know, he was the one who first lit the fuse for this society. For now, the initiators limited themselves to electing, as has been practiced since time immemorial, a board of directors. They elected: Bay Ganyo, of course, as chairman; Tanas Dochoolu, as the host, as vice-chairman; and Bay Taki as treasurer. Done! Who has ever heard or seen an election take place without a round of drinks? It’s not possible. That’s how it’s been, that’s how it is, and that’s how it will go. The vice-chairman, as the host, was the first to save face—he called the boy and whispered to him: "Two kilos of the old stuff, quickly!" They brought the wine. And what wine—is that even wine, that Sukhindol stuff—crystal, damn it all!...
— Well, cheers, may it be auspicious!
— Long live the chairman, hurrah!
— Thank you, long live His Royal Highness and the honorable government!
— Hooray!
— Down with drunkenness!...
Bay Ganyo also did himself proud. Bay Taki also did himself proud. And they repeated... and did it a third time... and so on until the onset of night...

It was already dark when I was walking with my companion along "Chista Rabota" Street. As we were passing by the Sukhindol Wines warehouse, an unusual noise coming from inside caught our attention and piqued our curiosity. We entered the warehouse, and through the small window of the inner room, this is the scene that shone before us: most of those gathered were snoring, sprawled out in no particular order on the chairs; Bai Taki, with his arms crossed over his belly, was snorting heavily with a drooping head and half-open eyes; a thin, tall gentleman, in a worn-out frock coat and blue spectacles, was turning in all directions and shouting into the void: "I am against machines, no matter what anyone says, I am against machines." Dochoolu was sitting at the table, his boy was holding a candle, and he was recording the bill in the notebook with a trembling hand. Bai Ganyo was pounding the table with all his might and, with a savage look, was screaming: "Me? I'll show them, I'll let them know who your Bai Ganyo is..." And Danko Harsizina, inspired by this energetic tone, had fixed his eyes on Bai Ganyo and seemed to be asking him with his gaze: "Just say it, Bai Ganyo, say it, brother, whom should I grab by the throat, whom should I kick out through the door?..."
The boy went out with the candle.
— Boy, what is this company? - asked my comrade.
— Society against drunkenness — the boy answered.
If there were prizes for the most carefree laughter to the point of breathlessness, then my companion and I would have received first prize at that moment.
Sofia, 12 May 1895
